overview: The atlas joins an Italian-colonial outline to a later Eritrea label beginning in 1960. That later date does not mark independence: Eritrea entered a federation with Ethiopia in 1952, was annexed in 1962, and became independent in 1993. These phases are distinguished here even where the imported outline stays similar.

periods.title: Federation with Ethiopia
periods.summary: The federation took effect in September 1952.

periods.title: Annexation and the independence struggle
periods.summary: Ethiopia dissolved the federation and annexed Eritrea in 1962.

periods.title: Independent Eritrea
periods.summary: The 1993 referendum preceded international recognition and formal independence celebrations.

items.text: The Italian colony dated from 1890 to 1941, so the map’s 1920 starting point is only a surviving snapshot. Colonial rule brought new administrative buildings and infrastructure, but it also placed Eritreans under an unequal political system. Its boundaries were not a map of a single language or people.

In September 1952 Eritrea became a federated unit under the Ethiopian Crown. Federation was different from independence and from outright annexation. The United Nations’ contemporary account records the arrangement and its promised integrity; the atlas’s 1960 label belongs to this phase.

Ethiopia annexed Eritrea in 1962. A long independence struggle eventually led to the 1993 referendum. Recognition and ceremony followed in stages: the United States recognized Eritrea on 27 April, while the official independence celebration took place on 24 May. A single year hides a sequence of political acts.

sections.title: Buildings that tell more than one story

items.text: Asmara’s surviving streets preserve colonial plans drawn between 1893 and 1941. Straight grids, radial roads and separate zones organized both activity and racial segregation. UNESCO also includes indigenous neighborhoods such as Arbate Asmera and Abbashawel, keeping African urban life visible beside the better-known colonial architecture.

The Fiat Tagliero service station, designed by Giuseppe Pettazzi in 1938, resembles an aircraft. Its freestanding concrete roof spans about 30 metres in the exhibition catalogue’s description. This was a place for cars with the appearance of a flying machine: dramatic engineering made an everyday fuel stop into a landmark.

Enda Mariam’s 1938 to 1939 church design incorporated local building traditions into its tower roofs, entrance and main structure. Asmara was not made by imported drawings alone. UNESCO emphasizes local construction knowledge, materials, skills and labor in the city’s development.

A dated writing sample is the Tigrinya newspaper masthead “ሓዳስ ኤርትራ”, meaning “New Eritrea”, on the 24 December 2025 issue of Haddas Ertra. Its letters use the Ethiopic script. This is modern state-published print, a different kind of evidence from an ancient inscription or an independent news report.

At Adi-Baro school, a July 2022 UNICEF account describes new separate toilets for girls and boys and a medical room with pads, detergent and disposal facilities. Fourteen-year-old Sesen Mihtreteab explained how privacy reduced anxiety about menstruation at school. Water came from a nearby reservoir into containers at the school and latrines.

Sesen also described returning to rope-skipping, football, volleyball and local games called Handay and Tempo while on her period. The report connects sanitation with being able to learn and play alongside classmates. The practical prize was an ordinary school day without avoidable embarrassment.

WHO’s report on 2024 describes disease surveillance as well as vaccination: health workers investigated suspected illness and laboratories tested 58 cases of acute flaccid paralysis, detecting no wild poliovirus. The report also recorded no measles outbreaks or measles-related deaths that year. These are dated monitoring results, not a declaration that every infection has disappeared.

Kerkebet Boarding School opened in 2022 to serve dispersed Bedawit communities. The UN’s 2025 results report describes solar-powered computer classrooms and pupils whose home villages could be as far as 200 kilometres away. Boarding, electricity and classrooms addressed different parts of the same challenge: making schooling reachable.

Independence did not guarantee political freedom. Human Rights Watch’s 2025 report describes restrictions on expression and indefinite national service, and notes that the 1997 constitution had not been implemented. Such conditions affect young people’s choices about education, work and family life, alongside the local improvements described above.

ending.text: Eritrea’s independent state emerged in 1993 after colonial rule, federation and annexation. Its people and cultural practices continued through those changes; the later state’s record also includes serious restrictions documented by rights monitors.
